analysis.one_liner: Caps flood insurance premiums for low-income households, small businesses, and nonprofits at 1% of area median income.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where it sat until the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require FEMA to give means-tested discounts on National Flood Insurance Program premiums. Eligible households earning up to 120% of area median income would pay no more than 1% of their area's median income for flood coverage on their primary home, and small businesses with up to 100 employees plus nonprofits could qualify through a hardship test. It also directs FEMA to let policyholders pay premiums in monthly installments, and funds the discounts with $250 million a year.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income homeowners in flood-prone areas — households at or below 120% of area median income — would see their flood insurance premiums capped at 1% of area median income. Small businesses with up to 100 employees and nonprofits that meet a hardship test would also qualify, and all policyholders would gain the option of paying premiums monthly rather than in a lump sum.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income flood-zone homeowners and small businesses

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual flood insurance premium for an eligible primary residence at no more than 1% of the area median income, protecting low- and moderate-income homeowners from steep premium increases.
Extends graduated discounts to small businesses with up to 100 employees and nonprofits that meet a hardship standard.
Requires FEMA to implement monthly installment payment of premiums — or explain to Congress why it cannot — easing the burden of large annual bills.
Appropriates $250 million a year to fund the discount program.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through a $250 million annual appropriation, and indirectly NFIP policyholders and the program itself if discounts must be funded from program revenues; the bill text provides general Treasury funding for the discounts.

drawbacks.text: The $250 million annual appropriation is subject to yearly congressional approval, and assistance ends once the fiscal year's money is spent — eligible policyholders have no guarantee of coverage discounts if funding lapses.

Capping premiums for the highest-risk low-income properties could push more costs onto the National Flood Insurance Program, which already carries substantial debt after major storms, unless appropriations fully cover the gap.
Eligibility depends on area median income, which in expensive coastal metros could extend discounts to households with six-figure incomes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real affordability problem — FEMA has been repricing flood insurance to full risk, and premiums of thousands of dollars a year can force people out of their homes or off coverage entirely. The discount cap plus a $250 million fund is a genuine, if modest, cushion, and the monthly payment option is a low-cost fix. The design is imperfect: the funding is capped and not guaranteed, and the income test is blunt. Overall the benefits to vulnerable homeowners outweigh the fiscal cost, which is small relative to the NFIP's scale.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Matt Cartwright introduced the National Flood Insurance Program Affordability Act on March 10, 2023.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, which held no further action on it.
The bill attracted two Democratic cosponsors and no additional action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed, so FEMA's existing premium structure stayed in place — meaning higher-income policyholders and the NFIP's current rate-setting were preserved, and low-income flood-zone homeowners got no relief from rising premiums.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; NFIP ratepayers saw no change

for.name: Rep. Matt Cartwright
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Financial Services Committee.

sides.party_line_note: No one opposed it on the record; it died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a floor fight, with only two cosponsors signing on.

industries.note: Low- and moderate-income policyholders would pay much less; if appropriations fell short of the discount fund, other policyholders could bear residual costs within the program.

industries.industry: FEMA and federal flood insurance program finances
industries.note: The program would take on $250 million in annual federal support while capping premiums on high-risk properties, softening the shift to full risk rates that was designed to put the program on sounder financial footing.

industries.industry: Private flood insurers and real estate interests in flood zones
industries.note: Cheaper public flood coverage keeps more homeowners insured, supporting home sales and lending in flood-prone areas, while reducing pressure on households to seek private-market alternatives.
